If anything, I tend to overthink and plan things out way too much rather than acting without considering the consequences.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how long this pattern of struggling to start tasks and getting easily distracted has been going on, and has it been consistent over time or does it vary?\n\nPatient: It’s been a constant, daily struggle for about the last two years, starting in my final semesters of college and continuing since I moved back home. It doesn't seem to make a difference.\n\nDoctor: When you're feeling overwhelmed by a task, can you tell me if the anxiety you experience is more about the task itself, such as fear of not doing it perfectly, or is it more about the broader consequences of not completing the task, like disappointing others or falling behind in life?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure which one it is, as I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. It feels like a mix of both, where I'm overwhelmed in the moment by the sheer effort of the task itself, but also constantly stressed about falling behind in life and letting my parents down.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your difficulty with starting tasks and getting distracted changes when you're under less pressure or stress, such as during a leisure activity, to help understand if your symptoms are more related to anxiety or attention issues?\n\nPatient: Honestly, I haven't really thought about how my focus or difficulty starting tasks changes during leisure activities versus when I'm under pressure. I'm not really sure if there is a noticeable difference, as I haven't compared them in that way.\n\nDoctor: Can you try to recall a recent situation where you were engaged in a leisure activity that you truly enjoyed, and see if you were able to focus and stay on task without significant distraction or difficulty, to help us understand how your symptoms might differ in low-pressure situations?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, as I haven't really thought about my focus in those moments. On the other hand, the frustration of not meeting my goals is a deep, constant weight that clashes with my self-image as a planner and makes me feel like my life is completely on hold. Both are intense, but the ongoing frustration of being stuck is what really wears me down day after day.\n\nDoctor: When you're able to momentarily overcome your resistance and start a task, do you feel like you're able to work steadily for a short period before getting distracted, or does the distraction and mental exhaustion hit you almost immediately after starting?"

I'm constantly stressed about not finishing my applications, being unemployed, and the growing tension it's causing with my parents. It just feels like my entire life is on hold right now, even though I have the qualifications to move forward.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself fidgeting, feeling restless, or having an urge to be constantly on the go, especially when you're supposed to be focusing on a task?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really experience physical restlessness or the urge to be constantly on the go. My struggle is much more about mental focus and feeling that heavy resistance to starting tasks. I tend to get easily distracted in my head rather than feeling physically hyperactive.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find yourself acting on impulse, such as interrupting others, blurting out answers, or doing things without much consideration for the consequences?\n\nPatient: No, I don't really act on impulse or interrupt others. If anything, I tend to overthink and plan things out way too much rather than acting without considering the consequences.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how long this pattern of struggling to start tasks and getting easily distracted has been going on, and has it been consistent over time or does it vary?\n\nPatient: It’s been a constant, daily struggle for about the last two years, starting in my final semesters of college and continuing since I moved back home. But looking back, this pattern actually goes all the way back to elementary school, where I’d constantly lose track of projects and get \"bright but careless\" comments on my report cards. It has always been a baseline issue for me, but it's become a massive roadblock now that I'm trying to complete these post-grad applications.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant periods in your life where you were able to focus and complete tasks without much difficulty, or has this pattern of inattention and distraction been relatively consistent throughout?\n\nPatient: It has been very consistent throughout my life, without any real periods where focusing was easy. Even in elementary school, I would constantly forget worksheets, lose track of projects, and get \"bright but careless\" comments on my report cards for skipping parts of assignments. The underlying struggle has always been there, but it became much more severe and stressful over the last two years once I lost the structured environment of school.\n\nDoctor: When you're able to finally start a task, do you find that your mind wanders due to a lack of interest in the task itself, or is it more because you're preoccupied with worries about not doing it perfectly or fear of failure?\n\nPatient: It's actually neither, because I genuinely want to complete these applications and it doesn't feel like perfectionism is blocking me. Instead, my mind just involuntarily drifts off to completely random things like googling train schedules or thinking about a movie. If I try to force myself to focus, I quickly feel a heavy, draining mental exhaustion.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever found yourself so engrossed in an activity that you lost track of time and were able to focus for an extended period without getting distracted?\n\nPatient: I’m not really sure, and I don’t think that happens much anymore. Even though I have a deep interest in art history, I usually find myself getting distracted or struggling to stay focused on a single task for long, rather than getting deeply engrossed in a productive way.\n\nDoctor: Can you recall any instances, perhaps related to a hobby or a specific interest, where you were able to maintain focus for an extended period without feeling distracted or mentally exhausted?\n\nPatient: I struggle to think of any hobbies or interests where I can maintain focus easily right now. Even though I love art history and analyzing art, when I try to sit down and write about it, I still find myself getting distracted by random things or feeling mentally exhausted pretty quickly.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any specific situations, tasks, or environments where you're able to focus and complete tasks without significant difficulty or distraction, which might help differentiate between your overall pattern of inattention and any potential situational factors?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, because it's hard to think of any environment or situation where focusing is easy for me right now. Even when I'm doing something I genuinely enjoy, like researching art or deep art criticism, I still run into that same heavy resistance and struggle to execute the concrete tasks. It doesn't seem to matter where I am or what I'm working on.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned struggling with focus across various tasks and environments, but can you think of any specific circumstances, such as working with others, having deadlines, or being in a highly structured setting, where your ability to focus and complete tasks might improve, even if slightly?\n\nPatient: I haven't really found any specific circumstances where my focus consistently improves. Even when I have deadlines or try to create highly structured schedules for myself, I still end up stalling, getting distracted, or feeling that heavy resistance to starting. It doesn't seem to make a difference.\n\nDoctor: When you're feeling overwhelmed by a task, can you tell me if the anxiety you experience is more about the task itself, such as fear of not doing it perfectly, or is it more about the broader consequences of not completing the task, like disappointing others or falling behind in life?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure which one it is, as I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. It feels like a mix of both, where I'm overwhelmed in the moment by the sheer effort of the task itself, but also constantly stressed about falling behind in life and letting my parents down.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your difficulty with starting tasks and getting distracted changes when you're under less pressure or stress, such as during a leisure activity, to help understand if your symptoms are more related to anxiety or attention issues?\n\nPatient: Honestly, I haven't really thought about how my focus or difficulty starting tasks changes during leisure activities versus when I'm under pressure. I'm not really sure if there is a noticeable difference, as I haven't compared them in that way.\n\nDoctor: Can you try to recall a recent situation where you were engaged in a leisure activity that you truly enjoyed, and see if you were able to focus and stay on task without significant distraction or difficulty, to help us understand how your symptoms might differ in low-pressure situations?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, as I haven't really thought about my focus in those moments. I suppose even when I'm doing things I enjoy, like reading about art or watching a movie, my mind still tends to drift off and I lose track of what I'm doing. It doesn't really feel like there's a big difference.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any persistent feelings of sadness, hopelessness, or a lack of interest in activities you once enjoyed, alongside your struggles with focus and task completion?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really felt persistent sadness or a loss of interest in things I enjoy. I do feel highly frustrated and stuck when it comes to my career and applications, but my passion for art history and museum studies is still very strong.\n\nDoctor: Can you try to rate the level of distress or anxiety you feel when you're unable to start or complete a task, compared to the frustration you feel about not meeting your goals or expectations?\n\nPatient: The distress of trying to start a task feels like an immediate, heavy mental block that completely drains my energy within just a few minutes of forcing myself to focus. On the other hand, the frustration of not meeting my goals is a deep, constant weight that clashes with my self-image as a planner and makes me feel like my life is completely on hold. Both are intense, but the ongoing frustration of being stuck is what really wears me down day after day.\n\nDoctor: When you're able to momentarily overcome your resistance and start a task, do you feel like you're able to work steadily for a short period before getting distracted, or does the distraction and mental exhaustion hit you almost immediately after starting?\n\nPatient: It hits me almost immediately. After only a few minutes of trying to force myself to focus, I feel completely drained and find myself looking for any excuse to get up. Other times, I'll suddenly realize I've been completely distracted by some random task, like googling something unrelated, without even realizing how I got off track.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your ability to focus and complete tasks changes when you're working on something that has a very clear, step-by-step process, versus something that requires more open-ended planning and organization?\n\nPatient: When tasks are open-ended and require self-directed planning, like application packets, I get completely overwhelmed, end up with too many tabs open, and struggle to break them into manageable steps or decide where to start. While highly structured tasks with clear external guidance are generally easier to handle, even when I try to create my own detailed, step-by-step plans, I still face a massive block when it's time to actually execute them.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulty with planning, organization, and self-regulation of your tasks is a significant part of your overall struggle with starting and completing tasks?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely, though the frustrating part is that I'm actually very thorough at making detailed plans and schedules beforehand. The real breakdown is in the execution and self-regulation; once I sit down, I struggle to organize the actual steps, end up bouncing between ten open tabs, and can't decide what to do first. That heavy resistance completely blocks me, preventing my careful plans from ever translating into completed tasks.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about how you plan and organize your daily tasks, and if you use any specific strategies or tools to help with this process, as it seems like planning isn't the issue but rather the execution?\n\nPatient: I actually put a lot of effort into organizing, using detailed schedules, custom systems, and filling my phone calendar with reminders. But when it's time to execute, it all falls apart because I get overwhelmed by too many open tabs and don't know where to start. I even end up forgetting or completely ignoring the very reminders I set, leaving me totally stuck.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced a period of at least two weeks where you felt persistently sad, empty, or lost interest in most activities, which could help differentiate between attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and a depressive disorder?\n\nPatient: No, I’ve never experienced a two-week period of feeling persistently sad, empty, or losing interest in things. My main struggles have always been more about getting started, staying focused, and organizing my tasks rather than feeling depressed.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any decrease in pleasure or interest in activities that you normally enjoy, outside of your struggles with task completion and focus?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really noticed any decrease in pleasure or interest in my favorite activities, like art history or movies. My struggle is purely with starting, focusing on, and completing structured tasks like my application packets.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you feel when you're in a situation where you're not expected to be productive or complete tasks, such as on a vacation or a relaxing weekend, and how your focus and anxiety levels compare to when you're facing deadlines or tasks?"

It doesn't seem to make a difference.\n\nDoctor: When you're feeling overwhelmed by a task, can you tell me if the anxiety you experience is more about the task itself, such as fear of not doing it perfectly, or is it more about the broader consequences of not completing the task, like disappointing others or falling behind in life?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure which one it is, as I haven't really thought about it in those exact terms. It feels like a mix of both, where I'm overwhelmed in the moment by the sheer effort of the task itself, but also constantly stressed about falling behind in life and letting my parents down.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your difficulty with starting tasks and getting distracted changes when you're under less pressure or stress, such as during a leisure activity, to help understand if your symptoms are more related to anxiety or attention issues?\n\nPatient: Honestly, I haven't really thought about how my focus or difficulty starting tasks changes during leisure activities versus when I'm under pressure. I'm not really sure if there is a noticeable difference, as I haven't compared them in that way.\n\nDoctor: Can you try to recall a recent situation where you were engaged in a leisure activity that you truly enjoyed, and see if you were able to focus and stay on task without significant distraction or difficulty, to help us understand how your symptoms might differ in low-pressure situations?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, as I haven't really thought about my focus in those moments. On the other hand, the frustration of not meeting my goals is a deep, constant weight that clashes with my self-image as a planner and makes me feel like my life is completely on hold. While highly structured tasks with clear external guidance are generally easier to handle, even when I try to create my own detailed, step-by-step plans, I still face a massive block when it's time to actually execute them.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulty with planning, organization, and self-regulation of your tasks is a significant part of your overall struggle with starting and completing tasks?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely, though the frustrating part is that I'm actually very thorough at making detailed plans and schedules beforehand. My struggle is purely with starting, focusing on, and completing structured tasks like my application packets.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you feel when you're in a situation where you're not expected to be productive or complete tasks, such as on a vacation or a relaxing weekend, and how your focus and anxiety levels compare to when you're facing deadlines or tasks?\n\nPatient: Honestly, I haven't really had a true vacation or a relaxing weekend in a long time because being unemployed makes me feel like I constantly *should* be working on applications.
